Schema: employees(id, name, dept, salary, manager_id, hired)

Show each employee with the average salary of their department next to it.

```sql
SELECT name, dept, salary,
       ROUND(AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept), 1) AS dept_avg
FROM employees
ORDER BY dept, salary DESC;
```

A window function keeps every employee row and adds the department average beside it. A plain GROUP BY would collapse each department to one row and lose the individual salaries.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
name  | dept  | salary | dept_avg
------+-------+--------+---------
Maya  | Eng   | 150    | 126.7   
Omar  | Eng   | 120    | 126.7   
Lena  | Eng   | 110    | 126.7   
Ivy   | Ops   | 80     | 72.5    
Ken   | Ops   | 65     | 72.5    
Sofia | Sales | 95     | 85.0    
Raj   | Sales | 90     | 85.0    
Tom   | Sales | 70     | 85.0    
```
I have employees(id, name, dept, salary, manager_id, hired). Who earns more than the average salary of the company?

```sql
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)
ORDER BY salary DESC;
```

The scalar subquery computes the company-wide average once, and the outer query compares each salary to it.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
name | salary
-----+-------
Maya | 150   
Omar | 120   
Lena | 110   
```

List each employee with their manager's name (employees without a manager should still appear).

Tables: employees(id, name, dept, salary, manager_id, hired) (SQLite)

```sql
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id
ORDER BY e.id;
```

This is a self-join: the same table appears twice under different aliases. LEFT JOIN keeps the top person (no manager), who gets NULL.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
employee | manager
---------+--------
Maya     | NULL   
Omar     | Maya   
Lena     | Maya   
Raj      | Maya   
Sofia    | Raj    
Tom      | Raj    
Ivy      | Maya   
Ken      | Ivy    
```

Using SQLite and these tables: employees(id, name, dept, salary, manager_id, hired).

Question: Show the whole reporting chain below Raj, with depth.

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE chain(id, name, depth) AS (
  SELECT id, name, 0 FROM employees WHERE name = 'Raj'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, c.depth + 1
  FROM employees e JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.id
)
SELECT name, depth FROM chain ORDER BY depth, name;
```

A recursive CTE starts from an anchor row (Raj) and repeatedly joins in rows whose manager is already in the result. It stops when no new rows are found.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
name  | depth
------+------
Raj   | 0    
Sofia | 1    
Tom   | 1    
```

Schema: employees(id, name, dept, salary, manager_id, hired)

Give the top earner of each department.

```sql
SELECT dept, name, salary
FROM (
  SELECT dept, name, salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn
  FROM employees
)
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY dept;
```

ROW_NUMBER numbers employees within each department by salary, and the outer filter keeps number 1. If you want ties kept, use RANK instead.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
dept  | name  | salary
------+-------+-------
Eng   | Maya  | 150   
Ops   | Ivy   | 80    
Sales | Sofia | 95    
```
I have employees(id, name, dept, salary, manager_id, hired). Label employees as junior, mid or senior by salary (below 80, 80 to 119, 120 and above).

```sql
SELECT name, salary,
       CASE
         WHEN salary < 80 THEN 'junior'
         WHEN salary < 120 THEN 'mid'
         ELSE 'senior'
       END AS band
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary;
```

CASE evaluates the conditions in order and returns the first match, so each later WHEN only applies to values not caught earlier.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
name  | salary | band  
------+--------+-------
Ken   | 65     | junior
Tom   | 70     | junior
Ivy   | 80     | mid   
Raj   | 90     | mid   
Sofia | 95     | mid   
Lena  | 110    | mid   
Omar  | 120    | senior
Maya  | 150    | senior
```

How many people were hired each year?

Tables: employees(id, name, dept, salary, manager_id, hired) (SQLite)

```sql
SELECT substr(hired, 1, 4) AS year, COUNT(*) AS hires
FROM employees
GROUP BY year
ORDER BY year;
```

SQLite stores dates as text here, so `substr(hired, 1, 4)` extracts the year. In other databases you would use EXTRACT or YEAR instead.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
year | hires
-----+------
2018 | 1    
2019 | 1    
2020 | 2    
2021 | 1    
2022 | 1    
2023 | 1    
2024 | 1    
```

Using SQLite and these tables: employees(id, name, dept, salary, manager_id, hired).

Question: Which departments have a total payroll above 200, and what is it?

```sql
SELECT dept, SUM(salary) AS payroll, COUNT(*) AS people
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept
HAVING SUM(salary) > 200
ORDER BY payroll DESC;
```

HAVING filters after aggregation, which WHERE cannot do because the sums do not exist yet when WHERE runs.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
dept  | payroll | people
------+---------+-------
Eng   | 380     | 3     
Sales | 255     | 3     
```

Schema: employees(id, name, dept, salary, manager_id, hired)

List each department's employees on one line.

```sql
SELECT dept, GROUP_CONCAT(name, ', ') AS people
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept
ORDER BY dept;
```

GROUP_CONCAT (SQLite; STRING_AGG in PostgreSQL and SQL Server) joins the values of each group into one string. The order inside the string is not guaranteed unless the database lets you specify it.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
dept  | people          
------+-----------------
Eng   | Maya, Omar, Lena
Ops   | Ivy, Ken        
Sales | Raj, Sofia, Tom 
```
I have employees(id, name, dept, salary, manager_id, hired). Show the salary gap between each employee and the next lower earner in their department.

```sql
SELECT dept, name, salary,
       salary - LEAD(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS gap_to_next
FROM employees
ORDER BY dept, salary DESC;
```

LEAD looks at the following row inside the window. The last person in each department has no next row, so the gap is NULL.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
dept  | name  | salary | gap_to_next
------+-------+--------+------------
Eng   | Maya  | 150    | 30         
Eng   | Omar  | 120    | 10         
Eng   | Lena  | 110    | NULL       
Ops   | Ivy   | 80     | 15         
Ops   | Ken   | 65     | NULL       
Sales | Sofia | 95     | 5          
Sales | Raj   | 90     | 20         
Sales | Tom   | 70     | NULL       
```

How many distinct users logged in each day?

Tables: events(id, user_id, kind, at) (SQLite)

```sql
SELECT at, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS users
FROM events
WHERE kind = 'login'
GROUP BY at
ORDER BY at;
```

COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) counts each user once per day, even if they logged in several times.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
at         | users
-----------+------
2025-01-01 | 1    
2025-01-02 | 1    
2025-01-03 | 2    
2025-01-06 | 2    
```

Using SQLite and these tables: events(id, user_id, kind, at).

Question: Which users logged in but never purchased?

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT user_id
FROM events
WHERE kind = 'login'
  AND user_id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM events WHERE kind = 'purchase')
ORDER BY user_id;
```

NOT IN with a subquery removes users who appear among the purchasers. Be careful: if the subquery can return NULL, NOT IN yields no rows at all, and NOT EXISTS is the safer pattern.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
user_id
-------
12     
```

Schema: events(id, user_id, kind, at)

Show each user's first and last event date and how many events they had.

```sql
SELECT user_id, MIN(at) AS first_day, MAX(at) AS last_day, COUNT(*) AS events
FROM events
GROUP BY user_id
ORDER BY user_id;
```

MIN and MAX work on text dates because ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD) strings sort in chronological order.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
user_id | first_day  | last_day   | events
--------+------------+------------+-------
10      | 2025-01-01 | 2025-01-06 | 5     
11      | 2025-01-02 | 2025-01-06 | 3     
12      | 2025-01-03 | 2025-01-05 | 2     
```
I have events(id, user_id, kind, at). For each user, what was the date of their previous event?

```sql
SELECT user_id, at, LAG(at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY at, id) AS previous_event
FROM events
ORDER BY user_id, at, id;
```

LAG returns a value from the previous row in the window, here the previous event for the same user. The first event per user gets NULL.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
user_id | at         | previous_event
--------+------------+---------------
10      | 2025-01-01 | NULL          
10      | 2025-01-01 | 2025-01-01    
10      | 2025-01-03 | 2025-01-01    
10      | 2025-01-05 | 2025-01-03    
10      | 2025-01-06 | 2025-01-05    
11      | 2025-01-02 | NULL          
11      | 2025-01-04 | 2025-01-02    
11      | 2025-01-06 | 2025-01-04    
12      | 2025-01-03 | NULL          
12      | 2025-01-05 | 2025-01-03    
```

Count events per kind as columns (one row for the whole table).

Tables: events(id, user_id, kind, at) (SQLite)

```sql
SELECT SUM(kind = 'login') AS logins,
       SUM(kind = 'view') AS views,
       SUM(kind = 'purchase') AS purchases
FROM events;
```

In SQLite a comparison yields 1 or 0, so summing it counts matches. This is a simple pivot; in other databases write `SUM(CASE WHEN kind = 'login' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
logins | views | purchases
-------+-------+----------
6      | 2     | 2        
```

Using SQLite and these tables: events(id, user_id, kind, at).

Question: Find days when there were more than 2 events.

```sql
WITH per_day AS (
  SELECT at, COUNT(*) AS n FROM events GROUP BY at
)
SELECT at, n FROM per_day WHERE n > 2 ORDER BY at;
```

A CTE gives the intermediate result a name, so the second step reads like plain filtering. It does the same job as HAVING here, but scales better to multi-step logic.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
at | n
---+--
```

Schema: products(id, name, stock, price) and sales(id, product_id, qty, day)

Which products are low on stock (under 10) and what have they sold?

```sql
SELECT p.name, p.stock, COALESCE(SUM(s.qty), 0) AS sold
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.product_id = p.id
WHERE p.stock < 10
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY p.name;
```

LEFT JOIN keeps products that never sold, and COALESCE turns the resulting NULL sum into 0.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
name    | stock | sold
--------+-------+-----
stapler | 5     | 2   
tape    | 0     | 0   
```
I have products(id, name, stock, price) and sales(id, product_id, qty, day). Compute revenue per product, highest first.

```sql
SELECT p.name, ROUND(SUM(s.qty * p.price), 2) AS revenue
FROM sales s
JOIN products p ON p.id = s.product_id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
```

Revenue is quantity times price per sale row, summed per product. Joining first makes the price available on every sale row.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
name     | revenue
---------+--------
pen      | 142.5  
notebook | 75.0   
stapler  | 24.0   
```

Which products have never been sold?

Tables: products(id, name, stock, price) and sales(id, product_id, qty, day) (SQLite)

```sql
SELECT name
FROM products p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sales s WHERE s.product_id = p.id);
```

NOT EXISTS checks, for each product, that no matching sale row is found. It handles NULLs more safely than NOT IN.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
name
----
tape
```

Using SQLite and these tables: products(id, name, stock, price) and sales(id, product_id, qty, day).

Question: Show a running total of units sold per product by day.

```sql
SELECT product_id, day, qty,
       SUM(qty) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY day, id) AS running_qty
FROM sales
ORDER BY product_id, day, id;
```

SUM as a window function with an ORDER BY accumulates from the start of the partition up to the current row.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
product_id | day        | qty | running_qty
-----------+------------+-----+------------
1          | 2025-02-01 | 30  | 30         
1          | 2025-02-02 | 25  | 55         
1          | 2025-02-03 | 40  | 95         
2          | 2025-02-01 | 10  | 10         
2          | 2025-02-03 | 15  | 25         
3          | 2025-02-02 | 2   | 2          
```

Schema: products(id, name, stock, price) and sales(id, product_id, qty, day)

What share of total units sold does each product account for?

```sql
SELECT p.name,
       SUM(s.qty) AS units,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(s.qty) / (SELECT SUM(qty) FROM sales), 1) AS pct
FROM sales s JOIN products p ON p.id = s.product_id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY units DESC;
```

The subquery supplies the grand total. Multiplying by 100.0 (not 100) forces decimal division instead of integer division.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
name     | units | pct 
---------+-------+-----
pen      | 95    | 77.9
notebook | 25    | 20.5
stapler  | 2     | 1.6 
```
I have products(id, name, stock, price) and sales(id, product_id, qty, day). Find the day with the highest total quantity sold.

```sql
SELECT day, SUM(qty) AS total
FROM sales
GROUP BY day
ORDER BY total DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

Group by day, sort the totals in descending order and keep the first row. Add a tie-break column if two days can share the top total.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
day        | total
-----------+------
2025-02-03 | 55   
```

Restock: set stock to at least 20 for every product that is below 20, and show the result.

Tables: products(id, name, stock, price) and sales(id, product_id, qty, day) (SQLite)

```sql
UPDATE products SET stock = MAX(stock, 20) WHERE stock < 20;
SELECT name, stock FROM products ORDER BY id;
```

In SQLite, scalar MAX with two arguments returns the larger value (other databases use GREATEST). Always put a WHERE clause on UPDATE, and try it first as a SELECT.

On a small sample dataset this returns:

```
name     | stock
---------+------
pen      | 100  
notebook | 40   
stapler  | 20   
tape     | 20   
```
My query is slow on a 5-million-row table: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10. What should I check?

Check the plan with EXPLAIN first. The usual fix is a composite index on `(customer_id, created_at)`: the database can jump to the customer's rows and read them already sorted, so it can stop after ten. Without it, it may scan the table or sort every matching row. Also avoid `SELECT *` if you need only a few columns, and confirm statistics are up to date. Measure before and after, since each index slows writes a little.
When should I use a CTE instead of a subquery?

Use a CTE when the query has several steps, when you reuse the same intermediate result, or when readability matters: it names each step. Use a subquery for a short one-off filter. Performance is usually equivalent in modern databases, but some engines materialise CTEs and others inline them, so check your database's behaviour if a query is slow.
Explain the difference between RANK, DENSE_RANK and ROW_NUMBER.

With scores 90, 90, 80: ROW_NUMBER gives 1, 2, 3 (always unique, ties broken arbitrarily). RANK gives 1, 1, 3 (ties share a rank and the next rank is skipped). DENSE_RANK gives 1, 1, 2 (ties share a rank, no gaps). Pick ROW_NUMBER to select exactly one row per group, RANK for competition-style ranking, and DENSE_RANK for 'top N distinct values'.
How do I do an upsert in SQLite or PostgreSQL?

Both support `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`. Example: `INSERT INTO counters(name, n) VALUES ('hits', 1) ON CONFLICT(name) DO UPDATE SET n = n + 1;`. The table needs a unique constraint or primary key on `name` for the conflict target. MySQL uses `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`, and SQL Server uses `MERGE`.
UNION vs UNION ALL?

UNION combines two result sets and removes duplicate rows, which requires extra work (a sort or hash). UNION ALL just appends them and keeps duplicates, and is faster. Use UNION ALL unless you actually need de-duplication. Both need the same number of columns with compatible types.
Should I store money as FLOAT?

No. Binary floating point can't represent many decimal fractions exactly, so sums drift (0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3). Store money as an integer number of the smallest unit (cents) or as a fixed-point DECIMAL/NUMERIC type, and keep the currency in a separate column.
What is the N+1 query problem?

It happens when code runs one query to fetch N parent rows, then one more query per parent to fetch its children, for N+1 round trips. It looks fine in development and becomes slow with real data. Fix it by fetching the related rows in one JOIN or with a single `WHERE parent_id IN (...)` query, or use your ORM's eager loading (for example `joinedload` or `selectinload` in SQLAlchemy).
Is it okay to use SELECT * in production code?

Avoid it in application queries. It transfers columns you don't need, breaks when columns are added or reordered, can defeat covering indexes, and may expose sensitive columns. It is fine for ad-hoc exploration in a console.
How do I safely run a big DELETE or UPDATE?

Write it first as a SELECT with the same WHERE clause and check the row count. Run it inside a transaction so you can roll back, and check the affected rows before committing. For very large tables, work in batches to avoid long locks, and make sure you have a recent backup. Never run an UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause unless you mean it.
What does a foreign key constraint buy me?

It makes the database enforce referential integrity: you can't insert an order for a customer that doesn't exist, and by default you can't delete a customer who still has orders (or you choose CASCADE, SET NULL, or RESTRICT). That moves a class of bugs out of application code. Note that SQLite only enforces foreign keys if you run `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` on each connection.
